column4: Abraham next sees the moon and watches it set; 6:76 begins the same night-covered sequence with a star, and this verse makes setting a repeated test of what can be divine.
The sun, larger than the moon, also sets, completing the sequence begun in 6:76; 6:79 then states Abraham's turn to the Creator of heaven and earth.
Abraham turns to the Creator after the star, moon, and sun have set; this completes 6:76-78's use of night to distinguish the setting from what remains.
Moses is promised forty nights before the people turn to the calf; this is another counted span of successive nights beside the section's plural ten nights.
Night is made for rest and day for sight; the verse gives a concrete human consequence of the section's covered darkness and opened visibility.
The counterfactual asks who could bring light if God made night perpetual; it reverses the section's dawn breaking the night-cover by imagining the break withheld.
The companion question asks who could bring night if God made day perpetual; it marks the other boundary of the cycle whose night-to-dawn edge opens the section.
Night enters into day and day into night; the verse gives another direct formulation of the two states passing through one another.
The verse again says that night enters day and day enters night, placing the section's slit of dawn within a recurring transition.
Night and day enter one another while sun and moon run to term; this develops the section's moving night as part of a measured cycle.
The same night-into-day and day-into-night motion is repeated alongside the sun and moon's appointed course, another specific formulation of the section's boundary crossing.
The oath by forenoon gives the bright side of the pairing; 93:2 presents night in stillness, so this ayah contributes the daylight counter-scene.

The name al-Hijr echoes the section's ḥijr, but this verse uses it as a place-name; its people deny messengers, while 15:82-83 supply the rock-carving and morning-destruction scene that links them to the surah's Thamud.
The people called Companions of al-Hijr carve homes into mountains and feel secure; this recalls 89:9's Thamud cutting rock, and 15:83 completes their fate at morning.

The same stone-carving people are seized by a cry at morning; this turns dawn into the hour of punishment, a counter-scene to the section's light breaking the night, while 15:82 supplies their carved homes.
One of the descriptions of Paradise is two gardens with branches; the garden word and boughs give a concrete leafy cover for the section's hidden, tree-covered jannah.
The gardens are dark green and dense; this gives another Quranic picture of the foliage that the section hears in the root ج ن ن.
The garden scene begins with thornless lote trees; 56:29-30 continue with clustered branches and extended shade, supplying the leafy shelter behind the section's final Garden image.
The next detail is clustered talh trees; 56:28 begins the same garden vegetation and 56:30 names its extended shade.
Extended shade covers the people of the right; 56:28-29 identify the trees, making this verse's shelter a concrete parallel to the section's covered Garden.

The verse describes a heart secure in faith even when the person is compelled to speak otherwise; this gives the section's tranquil soul a specific inward counterpart amid its contrast between moral rupture and faithful restraint.
The condemned say that listening or reasoning would have kept them from the Fire; this makes the section's “reason as inner wall” concrete as restraint that could have prevented transgression.
The destroyed generations' abandoned homes are a lesson for people of understanding; this connects the section's reason-as-restraint with the warning carried by the ruined peoples in surah 89.
The verse warns that crossing God's limits leads to the Fire; it states the consequence of failing the containing boundary that the section gives to ḥijr.
The faces of those who earned evil are covered with pieces of dark night; this makes darkness a judgment-cover, a moral counter-image to dawn's opening light.
The sky is split at the opening of the judgment scene; 82:4 later opens the graves, making this a cosmic tearing of the cover beside the section's dawn-rent night and buried earth.
The sky splits as the judgment begins; 84:3-4 continue with the earth opened and its contents cast out, a counter-scene joining the section's dawn rupture to its grave-cover image.
The earth is stretched out before it expels what lies within in 84:4; this gives the section's pounded earth a continuation from flattened ground to opened contents.
The earth is shaken violently, then 99:2 says it casts out its burdens; this completes the section's pounded-earth and grave-cover image as a single event.
